title: Shipyard and telecom workers
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The All India Shipyard Employees Federation and the Indian Telecom Employees Federation.
body:
Two of the smaller federations of Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) deserve closer attention: the **All India Shipyard Employees Federation** and the **Indian Telecom Employees Federation**. Both are listed among the 38 federations on the BMS website, and both represent workers in sectors that the country regards as strategic. Shipyards build the vessels that guard the coast and carry the trade; telecom is the network on which almost everything else now runs. Neither sector can function without skilled people, and in both the workers have lived through large changes. This post looks at each sector in turn, at the issues that concern the workers, and at what BMS's contribution is.

## Shipyards

India's shipyards, public and private, build naval vessels, commercial ships and offshore structures, and repair ships of many kinds. The main public yards include Mazagon Dock, Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers, Goa Shipyard, Cochin Shipyard and Hindustan Shipyard, and private groups such as Larsen & Toubro have also invested in yards. Indian shipbuilding is led mainly by naval work, which is dominated by public sector yards, while commercial shipbuilding has lagged. A business magazine report put India's share of world shipbuilding capacity at less than 1 per cent, with China, South Korea and Japan together holding about 98.5 per cent.

The Government has set out to change this. In September 2025 the Union Cabinet approved a package of Rs 69,725 crore for shipbuilding and the maritime sector. Its parts, as reported, include a shipbuilding financial assistance scheme running until 31 March 2036 with a fund of Rs 24,736 crore; a Maritime Development Fund of Rs 25,000 crore for long-term financing; and a Shipbuilding Development Scheme of Rs 19,989 crore to expand yards and clusters. The aim is to add about 4.5 million gross tonnage of annual shipbuilding capacity and attract about Rs 4.5 lakh crore of investment, with the Government expecting nearly 3 million jobs. A National Shipbuilding Mission is to oversee implementation.

For the worker, a shipyard is a place of skilled hands: welders, fitters, electricians, pipe-fitters, crane operators, draughtsmen and engineers. A ship is built block by block, and each block passes through many trades. That is why the supply of skilled people is a bottleneck. Observers note that skills are lost when orders dry up. The same magazine report points out that Mazagon Dock went about two decades without follow-on submarine orders and that Cochin Shipyard's aircraft-carrier line has stood idle since 2022, and that teams cannot be kept ready indefinitely without a steady flow of work.

### Issues in the yards

- **Contract workers' wages.** A large part of the work in yards is done by contractors' workers, who may be paid less than regular employees for similar tasks, with weaker benefits.
- **Safety in hull work and confined spaces.** Work inside tanks, double bottoms and engine rooms involves fire, fumes and limited escape. Cutting and welding near fuel residue is a serious risk. In February 2018 a blast on an ONGC drillship under repair at Cochin Shipyard killed five people. On 1 August 2020 a 70-tonne crane collapsed at Hindustan Shipyard during a load test and killed ten people, according to the global union federation IndustriALL, which said the victims included regular employees and workers of contractors. A report found that design and erection defects caused the collapse, and police registered a negligence case against the shipyard and two companies. The shipyard announced compensation of Rs 50 lakh to the families of permanent and contract workers killed and offered a job to a family member of each permanent employee who died. IndustriALL has urged unions to use the ILO's 2018 code of practice on safety and health in shipbuilding and ship repair for training.
- **Wage structures in defence shipyards.** Pay scales, allowances and settlement cycles in defence yards differ from those in other public enterprises, and workers raise questions of parity and of timely revision.
- **Growth and job security.** If the new package succeeds, new yards will open. The workers' organisation will ask whether the new jobs are regular, safe and well paid, or are mainly contract jobs.

## Telecom

Telecom employees have seen enormous change. The sector began as a government department, the Department of Telecommunications. Its services were later corporatised into Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) and Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL), and private operators entered the market and came to dominate it. The public companies were left to compete with an older network, a large workforce and heavy debt.

Government action followed in stages. A revival package of about Rs 70,000 crore in 2019 centred on a voluntary retirement scheme, restructuring of debt through sovereign guarantee bonds and monetisation of assets. According to a report on the 2022 package, over 92,000 BSNL and MTNL employees took voluntary retirement, which reduced the wage bill by about 50 per cent at BSNL and 75 per cent at MTNL. A second package, approved in July 2022 and reported at Rs 1.64 lakh crore, combined financial support, debt restructuring, viability-gap funding and administrative allotment of spectrum, and merged Bharat Broadband Network Limited into BSNL. A third package of Rs 89,047 crore, approved in June 2023, was mainly to give BSNL 4G and 5G spectrum. The Minister stated that combined support over five years was about Rs 3.22 lakh crore, that debt fell from Rs 32,944 crore to Rs 22,289 crore, and that the company recorded operating profits in 2020-21, 2021-22 and 2022-23. In September 2025 the Prime Minister inaugurated BSNL's indigenous 4G network with 97,500 towers.

### Issues in telecom

- **Revival of BSNL.** The workers have a direct stake in whether the investment of the past years leads to a lasting recovery. BMS, in its demands to the Government, has asked for full implementation of the BSNL and MTNL revival package.
- **Pensions and voluntary retirement.** Those who left under the scheme depend on pension arrangements, while those who stayed face a thinner organisation and heavier workloads.
- **Contract workers.** A network of towers, exchanges and cables is maintained by contract workers, whose wages have at times been delayed. In one case from Tamil Nadu, the Madras High Court directed BSNL to pay about 4,500 contract workers directly by the 15th of each month, with interest at 6 per cent a year on late payments, and to deduct and remit the contractors' provident fund, insurance and tax dues.
- **MTNL's future.** A memorandum of understanding on synergy of operations between MTNL and BSNL was signed in September 2024, which is not a merger and leaves open what will happen to MTNL's staff.

## Why they matter

Shipbuilding is key to maritime strength, because a country that cannot build and repair ships depends on others in time of need. Telecom is the nervous system of the digital economy, and a public operator in remote areas is often the only operator. Both need skilled people who are trained over years and who cannot be replaced overnight. When a sector is described as strategic, its workforce is part of the strategy.

## BMS's contribution

BMS's usual role is to bring such sectors into one national table, so that their issues can be placed before the labour and sector ministries in the same way as those of large industries. A shipyard worker in Visakhapatnam and a telecom technician in a district town may never meet, but belong to organisations that sit together and share experience of contract labour, safety and pension. That also allows BMS to raise common issues, such as the treatment of contract workers, in the wider discussion on labour codes.

## What remains to be done

For shipyards: a safety culture that treats contract and regular workers equally, with independent inspection after every serious accident; skills planning linked to the new orders; and regular employment for the new capacity. For telecom: a clear plan for BSNL and MTNL, with the future of the workers spelled out, secure pensions, and timely wages for contract workers.
